title: Many-Body Electronic Correlation Energy using Krylov Subspace Linear Solvers
problem: Direct computation of many-body electronic correlation energy via random-phase approximation exhibits quartic scaling with system size, creating severe computational inefficiencies. The approach requires solving block linear systems with complex symmetric coefficient matrices exhibiting widely-varying numerical difficulty and convergence behavior.
motivation: Efficient quantum chemistry simulations enable accurate materials discovery, drug design, and electronic structure prediction for complex chemical systems.
method: The approach breaks down the correlation energy calculation into linear systems solved together using a block Krylov subspace solver, a technique that iteratively refines the solution approximation. It automatically adjusts the batch size (how many equations to solve simultaneously) based on system difficulty—using larger batches when efficient and smaller batches when needed. This adaptive balancing reduces computational scaling from quartic to cubic and improves memory efficiency.
key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically choosing the right batch size for solving equations together, dynamically adjusting it to trade off per-iteration cost against convergence rate depending on problem difficulty.
contributions: RPA correlation energy formulation achieving cubic (vs quartic) scaling with system size
Short-term recurrence block Krylov subspace solver for complex symmetric linear systems
Dynamic block size selection mechanism to handle load imbalances from heterogeneous convergence
Demonstrated speedups over direct approaches with strong parallel scalability

metrics.speedup: Faster solution times than direct approaches on all tested systems; cubic vs quartic scaling enables larger system capability

limitations: Specific limitations of the proposed method are not discussed in the abstract.
primary_theme: Scalable quantum chemistry via adaptive Krylov subspace linear solvers
